title: Interpreters and Compilers
tagline: How source code becomes execution — from pure interpretation to ahead-of-time compilation, bytecode VMs, and JIT.

sections.content:
You write `let x = 6 * 7` and the computer executes it. But a CPU has no idea what `let`, `x`, `*`, or `7` mean. All it understands is a stream of tiny, primitive machine instructions like `MOV R1, 6`, `MUL R1, 7`, `STORE R1, [addr]`. Something in between must bridge your human-readable text and those raw instructions. That something is either an **interpreter** or a **compiler** — and the design decision made here has sweeping consequences for every program ever run on every device.

This is not a theoretical curiosity. The execution strategy your runtime chooses determines your program's startup latency, peak throughput, portability to other hardware, ability to use dynamic features like `eval()`, and even your security posture (JIT spray attacks exploit the JIT compiler). Understanding interpreters and compilers means understanding *why* Python feels slow for CPU-bound work, why Java's JVM was once mocked for startup time but now comes close to C++ throughput in long-running servers, why Rust binaries start instantly, and why JavaScript in a browser often runs within a small factor of compiled code today.

At the highest level there are three pure strategies: **direct interpretation** (visit the source AST and execute it immediately), **compilation** (transform the program into a lower-level form before running it), and the critically important hybrid — **JIT compilation** (compile while running, guided by runtime profiling). Real runtimes combine all three in sophisticated pipelines. V8, the JavaScript engine in Chrome and Node.js, compiles every function to bytecode for its interpreter (Ignition), then promotes warm functions through a quick baseline compiler (Sparkplug), a mid-tier optimiser (Maglev), and a top-tier optimiser (TurboFan) — all within the same run of a single file, with functions moving between tiers as their behaviour changes.

By the end of this chapter you will understand how each strategy works mechanically, why each exists, the exact tradeoffs they make, and how to reason about which one a given language runtime uses and why.

sections.caption: The four execution strategies all start from the same AST. They differ only in how many transformation steps happen before instructions actually execute.

sections.title: Translating a Foreign Book — Four Different Strategies
sections.content:
Imagine you have a French novel you want to understand. You hire four different translation teams.

**Team 1 — Pure Interpreter**: A translator sits next to you, reads each French sentence aloud in English *on the spot*. You understand immediately, but every time you flip back to page 12, they translate it all over again from scratch. Perfect for a book you will read once, painful for one you consult constantly.

**Team 2 — Bytecode VM**: The translator first produces a rough draft in a compact shorthand — not full English, not French, but a middle-ground notation that is much faster for the translator to read than French. From now on the translator works from the shorthand, not the original. Repeated reads are faster; you also get to store the shorthand on disk so you never re-translate from French again.

**Team 3 — JIT Compiler**: You start with the shorthand (bytecode), and your assistant notices that you keep rereading Chapter 7. They disappear for an hour and return with a perfect, fully polished English version of Chapter 7. Now you read Chapter 7 at full English speed, while the rest of the book is still read from shorthand. The improvement is proportional to how often each chapter is accessed.

**Team 4 — AOT Compiler**: Before you ever open the book, the publisher has produced a complete English edition. When you sit down to read, it is already fully translated — maximum reading speed from page one, but you waited for the full translation before you could start at all, and this English edition only works for English readers (not Portuguese ones).

sections.title: Tree-Walking Interpretation: The Simplest Strategy
sections.content:
A **tree-walking interpreter** is the most direct way to execute a program. After the source text is parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), the interpreter visits each node and immediately performs the corresponding action. There is no intermediate compilation step.

The mechanism is a recursive `eval()` function. When `eval` visits a `Literal` node it returns the number. When it visits a `BinaryExpression` node it recursively evaluates the left and right children, then applies the operator. When it visits an `IfStatement` it evaluates the condition and then visits either the consequent or alternate branch. Variables are stored in an **environment** — a dictionary (or linked list of dictionaries for lexical scoping) mapping names to values.

The beauty of tree-walking is simplicity. You can build a working interpreter for a modest language in a few hundred lines. Ruby before 1.9 (the YARV bytecode VM arrived in 2007), many `esprima`/`acorn`-based JavaScript sandboxes, configuration and template languages, and most teaching interpreters work this way. The Python `ast.literal_eval` function is a tree-walker.

**Why it is slow for hot code**: Consider a loop that iterates 10,000 times. Every single iteration the interpreter re-traverses the same AST nodes — checking the node type with a `switch`, following pointer chains through the tree, dispatching to the right case. This overhead is proportional to *both* the number of iterations and the structural complexity of the loop body. The tree never changes, but it is walked every time. Bytecode VMs fix exactly this problem.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `eval()` method is the entire interpreter. Each recursive call handles exactly one AST node. The environment object (`this.env`) is the variable scope — a real implementation would chain environments for nested scopes. Notice that even the loop `for (const stmt of node.body)` is a JavaScript loop, meaning the host language (JS) is doing the work for each iteration of the interpreted language — this is the fundamental overhead of tree-walking.

sections.title: Bytecode and Virtual Machines: Flattening the Tree
sections.content:
The key insight behind bytecode VMs: an AST is a **tree** (pointer-rich, heap-allocated, slow to traverse), but what we actually need to execute is a **sequence** of simple operations. If we can flatten the tree into a linear list of instructions once, we can then execute that list repeatedly much faster.

**Bytecode** is that flat instruction list. Each instruction is a simple, compact operation: `PUSH 6`, `PUSH 7`, `MUL`, `STORE area`. The virtual machine that executes bytecode is just a loop: read the next instruction (indexed by a program counter integer), dispatch on the opcode, update a stack or set of registers, advance the PC. No pointer chasing through tree nodes and no recursive calls — just one dispatch per instruction.

This is why the term **stack machine** appears so often. Most bytecode VMs use a stack as their primary data structure. The operands for an operation are pushed onto the stack; the operation pops them, computes the result, and pushes it back. Python's `dis` module lets you see CPython's bytecode; Java's `javap -c` shows JVM bytecode. These are not machine code — they are instructions for a *virtual* machine defined in software.

**Bytecode caching** is a major practical benefit. Python compiles source to bytecode and stores it in `.pyc` files inside `__pycache__`. On the next run, if the source has not changed, Python loads the cached bytecode directly, skipping lexing, parsing, and AST construction. For large codebases this saves seconds on startup. Java's `.class` files are bytecode; once compiled by `javac`, the same `.class` file runs on any JVM — Windows, Linux, macOS, x86 or ARM. (Android is the exception that proves the rule: its build converts `.class` files to its own DEX bytecode for the ART runtime.) This is the famous **write once, run anywhere** portability.

**Register-based VMs** are an alternative to stack machines. Instead of a stack, they use a fixed set of virtual registers (like `r0`, `r1`, `r2`). Lua 5.0 switched from a stack VM to a register VM specifically to reduce instruction count — fewer `PUSH`/`POP` instructions are needed when you can write `ADD r3, r1, r2` directly. Android's Dalvik VM (now replaced by ART) was also register-based. Register VMs tend to execute fewer instructions per operation but each instruction is larger (it must encode register names).

sections.caption: Compiling a BinaryExpression to bytecode produces a flat instruction list. The VM loop executes it without tree traversal — each instruction is just an array index increment.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The compile pass runs once and converts the pointer-rich AST into a plain array of instruction objects. The VM loop is trivially simple — it is just `for ... switch` over that array. A real bytecode VM would encode opcodes as integers (not strings) and arguments as packed bytes for cache efficiency, but the logic is identical. Notice that STORE pops the top of the stack into the environment and LOAD pushes an environment value onto the stack — this is how variables cross the boundary between the stack and persistent storage.

sections.title: JIT Compilation: Profiling and Specialising Hot Code
sections.content:
Bytecode interpretation is faster than tree-walking, but there is still a fundamental overhead: for every bytecode instruction executed, the VM loop must check the opcode, branch to the right handler, and manipulate a software stack. A real CPU could execute the same operation in a single instruction if the code were compiled to native machine code.

**Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation** solves this. A JIT compiler runs *inside the process, while the program is executing*. It monitors which functions or loops are called frequently — these are called **hot paths** — and when a path becomes hot (exceeds a threshold like 1,000 executions), the JIT compiles it to native machine code on the fly. From then on, every call to that function runs the native code directly, bypassing the VM loop entirely.

**Type specialisation** is what makes JIT-compiled code genuinely fast — sometimes faster than statically compiled C code. When the JIT observes that a particular function has always been called with integer arguments, it generates machine code specialised for integers: direct CPU `ADD` and `MUL` instructions with no type-checking overhead. A static AOT compiler must generate code that handles *any* possible argument type; the JIT can generate code for the *observed* types. This is the key reason JIT-compiled JavaScript can rival C for number-crunching loops.

**Deoptimisation** is the flip side. JIT-compiled code is built on assumptions derived from profiling data. If those assumptions are later violated — for example, a function that always received integers is suddenly called with a string — the JIT must **deoptimise**: discard the native code, patch in the slower bytecode interpreter for this function, and possibly collect new profiling data to re-JIT with a wider type assumption. In V8, optimised Maglev or TurboFan code deoptimises back to the Ignition interpreter, which reconstructs the interpreter frame mid-function and carries on. HotSpot JVM calls it an uncommon trap. Deoptimisation loops (where code oscillates between JIT and deopt) are a real source of JavaScript performance bugs.

**Warmup time** is the period before the JIT kicks in. A fresh process starts in interpreter mode, which is slower. For long-running servers (Java application servers, Node.js APIs) this is fine — they warm up over the first few seconds of traffic. For short-lived scripts (CLI tools, serverless functions) the JIT may never fully kick in, and startup/warmup latency dominates performance. This is why the Go language chose AOT over JIT: Go targets servers and CLIs where startup speed matters more than peak throughput.

sections.caption: V8's four tiers (2026). Every function starts as Ignition bytecode; Sparkplug turns bytecode into machine code almost for free; Maglev and TurboFan speculate on the observed types and shapes, guarded by checks. A failed check deoptimises back to Ignition, and the function can tier up again later with broader feedback.

sections.title: AOT Compilation: Translating Everything Before Execution
sections.content:
**Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation** moves the entire translation burden before the program runs. The compiler reads source code, performs full semantic analysis, type-checking, and optimisation, and emits native machine code (an ELF binary on Linux, a Mach-O binary on macOS, a PE/COFF `.exe` on Windows). When you run the binary, the CPU executes the native instructions directly — no parser, no interpreter, no VM loop, no JIT warmup.

Languages that use AOT compilation include C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift, and Fortran. The compiler (GCC, Clang, rustc, the Go toolchain) is a separate tool that runs in the development environment, not at runtime. The shipped binary has no dependency on any runtime beyond the operating system's system libraries.

**The optimisation advantage**: AOT compilers have unlimited time to optimise. LLVM's optimisation pipeline includes inlining, loop unrolling, dead code elimination, vectorisation (using SIMD instructions), and dozens of other passes. A Rust release build (`cargo build --release`, i.e. `-C opt-level=3`) runs a long LLVM pass pipeline, often for minutes on a large crate. A JIT compiles on background threads while the program runs, but its budget is still milliseconds per function, so it must pick its optimisations carefully.

**The portability cost**: native machine code is CPU-architecture-specific. An x86-64 binary does not run on ARM64 (Apple Silicon) without emulation. An AOT-compiled C program must be cross-compiled for each target platform. This was considered an acceptable tradeoff in the systems programming world but a fatal limitation for widely distributed software — which is exactly why the JVM's bytecode portability was revolutionary for Java in 1995.

**Ahead-of-time in JVM and .NET**: The JVM traditionally used JIT, but newer systems like GraalVM Native Image and .NET's NativeAOT compile to native code ahead of time for serverless and container use-cases where startup latency matters. Android's ART runtime combines all the strategies: apps start interpreted and JIT-compiled, ART records which methods are hot, and the `dex2oat` compiler AOT-compiles those methods while the device is idle and charging (shipped 'baseline profiles' let apps get AOT code for their startup path from the first launch).

**Link-Time Optimisation (LTO)**: A powerful AOT technique where the compiler sees the entire program (not just each translation unit in isolation) during the final link step. This allows inlining across module boundaries and whole-program dead code elimination. Rust enables this via `lto = true` in Cargo.toml.

sections.title: The Tradeoffs in Detail: Choosing the Right Strategy
sections.content:
No single strategy is universally best. Each is an engineering tradeoff along several dimensions.

**Startup latency vs peak throughput**: Tree-walkers start instantly but are slow under load. AOT binaries also start almost instantly (no compilation at runtime) and peak fastest. JIT runtimes start in their interpreter, so startup is decent but early execution is slow; after warmup they can approach — and on dynamic workloads occasionally beat — AOT code. Bytecode VMs are in the middle on both dimensions.

**Portability**: Bytecode VMs offer the highest portability because the VM itself is the architecture-specific component, not the bytecode. Java `.class` files, Python `.pyc` files, and JavaScript bundles are all portable across any platform that ships the VM. AOT binaries are architecture-locked. Tree-walkers are portable if the interpreter itself is portable.

**Dynamic language features**: `eval()`, `exec()`, dynamic module loading, hot code reloading, live patching — all of these are easy for interpreters (you already have the parser and environment in memory) and painful for AOT compilers (the binary does not include a compiler). This is why Python can do `exec('x = 1 + 2')` trivially, but Rust cannot execute arbitrary Rust source at runtime without shipping a full Rust compiler. JIT runtimes can support `eval()` by passing the dynamically generated code through the normal bytecode + JIT pipeline.

**Memory overhead**: JIT compilers allocate memory for compiled native code at runtime (the JIT code cache). HotSpot's code cache is typically hundreds of megabytes (240 MB reserved by default with tiered compilation). AOT binaries are fixed-size; all code is in the binary, not in heap memory. For constrained embedded environments (IoT, microcontrollers), AOT is often the only viable option.

**Debugging and instrumentation**: Interpreters make excellent debuggers because execution is driven by the host language — you can pause at any AST node, inspect the environment, and resume. AOT binaries require separate debug info (DWARF tables) to map machine code addresses back to source lines. JIT debuggability is the worst because the native code exists only in memory and may be invalidated by deoptimisation.

**Security**: JIT compilation creates executable memory pages at runtime. This is a known attack surface — JIT spray attacks inject attacker-controlled values into JIT-compiled code to create useful instruction sequences. Modern JITs enforce `W^X` (write XOR execute) by flipping page permissions between writing and running code, but JIT compiler bugs remain among the most exploited browser vulnerabilities, because a wrong speculation can produce memory-unsafe machine code. Some platforms forbid JIT outright: on iOS only Apple-entitled engines may JIT, and hardened modes such as Edge's enhanced security or V8's `--jitless` trade speed for a smaller attack surface.

sections.title: Real-World Runtimes: How They Actually Work
sections.content:
Understanding abstract strategies is clarified enormously by mapping them to real systems you interact with daily.

**CPython** (the standard Python implementation): When you run `python script.py`, CPython lexes, parses to an AST, compiles the AST to bytecode (CPython's own instruction set, viewable with `import dis; dis.dis(fn)`), and then interprets that bytecode in a C-implemented evaluation loop. Since Python 3.11 the loop is a *specialising adaptive interpreter* (PEP 659): hot instructions rewrite themselves into type-specific variants, a big step toward JIT-style speculation. Python 3.13 added an experimental copy-and-patch JIT as a build option, and the official 3.14 Windows and macOS binaries include it, off by default (`PYTHON_JIT=1` turns it on); it is still experimental, with modest speedups so far. Separately, 3.14 made the **free-threaded (no-GIL) build** officially supported (PEP 779) — still an optional, separate build (`python3.14t`), not the default. The `.pyc` file in `__pycache__` is the cached bytecode. CPython's speed for CPU-bound work is limited by this interpretation overhead — hence why NumPy, pandas, and PyTorch drop into C extensions for hot loops.

**JVM / HotSpot** (Java, Kotlin, Scala, Clojure): `javac` compiles source to JVM bytecode (`.class` files). The JVM interprets this bytecode initially. HotSpot's tiered compilation then promotes hot methods through C1 (fast, low-quality JIT) and C2 (slow, high-quality JIT) compilers. GraalVM's JIT is written in Java itself. After warmup, JVM throughput is often within a small factor of C/C++, and sometimes on par.

**V8** (Chrome, Node.js, Deno): four tiers. **Ignition** compiles every function to bytecode for a register machine with an accumulator and interprets it while collecting type feedback. **Sparkplug** (2021) is a baseline compiler that translates bytecode straight to machine code with no optimisation — compiling is nearly free, and it removes interpreter dispatch overhead. **Maglev** (2023) is a fast mid-tier optimising compiler that uses the feedback to specialise code. **TurboFan** is the top-tier optimiser for the hottest code; V8 has been moving it off its original 'sea of nodes' IR: since 2025 TurboFan's entire backend runs on a CFG-based IR called Turboshaft, and its JavaScript frontend is being replaced by Maglev's CFG-based graph. Optimised code deoptimises back to Ignition when its assumptions break. (WebAssembly has its own pair: the Liftoff baseline compiler and an optimising tier whose pipeline is now fully Turboshaft.)

**Rustc / GCC / Clang**: Pure AOT compilers. All analysis, type-checking, and optimisation happen before the binary ships. No runtime component beyond the OS. Programs start in microseconds.

**Lua**: Lua has always compiled to bytecode; Lua 5.0 (2003) switched its VM from stack-based to register-based, and that design remains the core today. LuaJIT is a third-party JIT compiler for Lua that is among the fastest scripting language runtimes ever produced, demonstrating what a well-engineered JIT can achieve.

**WebAssembly (WASM)**: A bytecode format designed as a compilation target for browsers. It ships pre-compiled from C, Rust, Go, etc. Browsers JIT-compile WASM to native code at load time. WASM is essentially an AOT-compiled portable bytecode — it combines AOT's pre-compilation with bytecode's portability, getting near-native speed in browsers without the portability cost of native binaries.

sections.title: Inside the JIT: Profiling, Type Feedback, and Inline Caches
sections.content:
Modern JIT compilers are surprisingly sophisticated. Understanding three specific mechanisms explains why they can generate such fast code.

**Call count profiling**: The simplest JIT trigger. A counter is associated with each function or loop header in the bytecode. The interpreter increments the counter on every entry. When the counter crosses a threshold, the function is submitted to the JIT compiler. (V8 actually uses an 'interrupt budget' weighted by how much bytecode runs, rather than a raw call count, so big functions tier up after fewer calls.)

**Type feedback and speculation**: The interpreter tracks the types of values seen at each operation site. For a `+` instruction that has always seen two 32-bit integers, the JIT generates native `ADD` instructions with no type checks. It places a guard right before the specialised operation: `if (!isSmallInt(a) || !isSmallInt(b)) DEOPT`, plus an overflow check on the add. Each guard is a well-predicted branch that costs almost nothing while the assumption holds.

**Inline caches (ICs)**: Property access in dynamic languages like JS is expensive — `obj.x` might require a hash table lookup. An inline cache replaces the generic lookup with a specialised one: it records the object's **hidden class** (V8's internal description of an object's shape — which properties it has, in what order) and generates direct memory offset access if the same shape is seen again. `obj.x` becomes `load memory[obj_ptr + offset_of_x]` — a single memory read. If the object's shape changes (a new property is added), the IC misses and falls back to the slow path.

These three mechanisms together explain V8's performance: for code that works with consistent types and object shapes, V8 effectively generates code indistinguishable from hand-written C. For code with wild polymorphism (different types every call), V8 stays in the slower interpreter or generates pessimistic native code with many type checks.

sections.label: Watching V8 tier up
sections.code:
# hot.js
#   function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
#   let s = 0;
#   for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) s = add(s, i);   // integers only
#   add('x', 'y');                                   // breaks the assumption
#   for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) s = add(s, i);

# 1. See Ignition's bytecode (a register machine with an accumulator)
node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=add hot.js
#   Ldar a1          ; load argument b into the accumulator
#   Add a0, [0]      ; accumulator = a + accumulator, type feedback slot [0]
#   Return

# 2. Watch tier-up and deoptimisation (output trimmed, Node 23)
node --trace-opt --trace-deopt hot.js
#   [marking add for optimization to MAGLEV ... reason: hot and stable]
#   [bailout (kind: deopt-eager, reason: not a Smi): ... deoptimizing add]
#   [marking add for optimization to MAGLEV ... reason: hot and stable]
#   [marking add for optimization to TURBOFAN ... reason: hot and stable]

# 3. Run with every JIT tier disabled (interpreter only) — slower, smaller attack surface
node --jitless hot.js
sections.explanation: These are real V8 flags (output from Node 23, trimmed). The trace shows the whole lifecycle from this chapter: `add` gets hot on integers and is optimised by Maglev; the single string call violates the 'small integer' (Smi) speculation, so the code bails out to Ignition; with broadened feedback it is re-optimised by Maglev and finally TurboFan. Flags like these are internal and change between versions — use them to explore, not in production.

sections.content: **Historical context worth knowing**: The first compiler was written by Grace Hopper in 1952 (A-0 system for UNIVAC I). The idea was controversial — programmers argued that no compiler could produce code as efficient as hand-written assembly. They were mostly right in 1952 and are mostly wrong today. Modern LLVM and GCC optimisers routinely produce code faster than expert hand-written assembly for non-trivial programs because they apply dozens of transformations in sequence that no human could maintain simultaneously. JIT ideas go back to 1960s Lisp systems, but the modern design comes from Smalltalk-80 (Deutsch and Schiffman, 1984) and especially **Self** (Stanford and Sun, late 1980s–1990s), which pioneered type feedback, inline caches, and deoptimisation. Self's engineers went on to build Strongtalk and then **HotSpot**, and the same ideas — via engineers like Lars Bak — shaped V8.

**Common misconceptions and interview traps**: (1) 'Interpreted languages are always slow' — modern JIT-compiled JS/Java/C# match C for many workloads. The real cost is startup and warmup, not peak throughput. (2) 'Python is interpreted' — CPython compiles to bytecode first; the 'interpreted' part is the bytecode VM, not direct AST traversal. (3) 'JIT is always better than AOT' — for short-lived scripts, serverless functions, and CLIs, JIT's warmup overhead makes AOT preferable (see: Go, Rust, Zig). (4) 'Deoptimisation is free' — each deopt flushes compiled code for a function, causes a mode switch, and requires re-profiling. Pathological deopt loops (monomorphic → polymorphic type change → compile → deopt → compile again) are a real performance hazard in JavaScript. (5) 'Bytecode is machine code' — bytecode is for a *virtual* machine; machine code is for a real CPU. They differ in portability, execution speed, and the need for a VM runtime.

items: **Tree-walking interpreters** execute AST nodes directly with a recursive `eval()` function — the simplest design, instant startup, but slow for hot loops because the tree is re-traversed on every iteration.

**Bytecode VMs** compile the AST to a flat, linear instruction list once, then execute that list in a tight VM loop. Bytecode caching (`.pyc`, `.class`) skips re-compilation on subsequent runs. Write-once-run-anywhere portability is the key benefit.

**JIT compilers** profile running bytecode to identify hot paths, then compile only those paths to native machine code using type specialisation and inline caches — achieving near-AOT speed after warmup, occasionally faster than static AOT thanks to runtime type information.

**AOT compilers** (Rust, C, Go) translate everything to native machine code before the program runs — fastest startup, highest peak throughput, access to deep optimisation passes, but binaries are architecture-specific and dynamic features like `eval()` are severely limited.
**CPython** compiles to bytecode (cached in `.pyc`) and runs a specialising adaptive interpreter (3.11+); its copy-and-patch JIT (3.13+) is still experimental and off by default.

**Deoptimisation** is the JIT safety valve: when type assumptions break, the JIT discards its compiled code and falls back to the bytecode interpreter — essential for correctness in dynamic languages but a potential performance hazard if it loops.

**V8 uses four tiers**: Ignition (bytecode interpreter + type feedback), Sparkplug (non-optimising baseline compiler), Maglev (mid-tier optimiser), and TurboFan (top-tier optimiser) — each trading compile time for speed; optimised code deoptimises back to Ignition.

**Real-world choice**: use the runtime that matches your workload's constraints — AOT for CLIs and embedded (startup matters), JIT for long-running servers (peak throughput matters), bytecode VM for portability across architectures, and tree-walkers for sandboxed scripting or educational interpreters.

quiz.question: What is the defining characteristic of a pure tree-walking interpreter compared to other execution strategies?
options: It compiles the AST to native machine code in a separate step before any code runs.
It converts source code to bytecode and interprets that bytecode in a VM loop.
It visits AST nodes directly and executes corresponding operations immediately, with no intermediate compilation step.
It profiles running code and emits native instructions only for frequently called functions.
quiz.explanation: A tree-walking interpreter's defining trait is executing the AST directly via recursive node traversal. There is no compilation step whatsoever — the AST structure itself drives execution. This is simple to implement but slow for repeated execution because the same tree nodes are traversed on every iteration.

quiz.question: Why is bytecode interpretation generally faster than tree-walking interpretation for code inside a loop?
options: Bytecode is a flat array of simple instructions with an integer program counter, eliminating recursive pointer traversal of the AST on each loop iteration.
Bytecode uses hardware-accelerated virtual machine instructions.
Bytecode compiles directly to machine code so no interpreter is needed.
Bytecode caches results from previous loop iterations to avoid re-computation.
quiz.explanation: The tree-walker must re-traverse pointer-linked AST nodes on every loop iteration. Bytecode is a flat array indexed by a simple integer (the program counter). Dispatching on an opcode in an array is dramatically cheaper than following heap pointers and recursively dispatching on node types. The tree is walked once to produce bytecode; subsequent iterations just step through the flat array.

quiz.question: What does a JIT compiler use to decide which bytecode functions to compile to native machine code?
options: Static analysis of the source code performed at compile time.
A developer annotation in the source code such as @hot or @jit.
The file size of the bytecode: smaller files are compiled, larger files are interpreted.
Runtime profiling — counting how many times each function or loop is executed and compiling those that exceed a threshold.
quiz.explanation: JIT compilers identify 'hot paths' through runtime profiling — incrementing execution counters for functions and loop back-edges. When a counter exceeds a configured threshold, the JIT compiler is triggered for that code. This is why JIT-compiled programs have a warmup period: the JIT only kicks in after sufficient profiling data has been collected.

quiz.question: V8's TurboFan JIT compiler can 'deoptimise' a function. What triggers deoptimisation?
options: The function has been running in native code for more than one second.
A type assumption made during JIT compilation — such as 'this argument is always an integer' — is violated by a new call with a different type.
The JavaScript garbage collector needs to reclaim the memory used by native code.
The user explicitly calls the browser's DevTools memory profiler.
quiz.explanation: TurboFan generates specialised native code based on observed type profiles (type speculation). Each compiled function contains guards checking that types match the speculated profile. If a call violates a guard (e.g., a function profiled as integer-only receives a string), V8 deoptimises: it discards the TurboFan code for that function and reverts to Ignition bytecode interpretation, possibly re-profiling for a less-specialised recompilation.

quiz.question: Python's CPython runtime stores compiled bytecode in `.pyc` files. What specific benefit does this provide?
options: It skips lexing, parsing, and AST-to-bytecode compilation on subsequent runs when the source file has not changed, improving startup time.
It encrypts the source code so it cannot be read by end users.
It enables JIT compilation on the next run without needing the source file.
It converts Python bytecode to native machine code for the specific CPU architecture.
quiz.explanation: CPython caches bytecode in `.pyc` files (inside `__pycache__`). On startup, CPython checks whether the source file has changed (by comparing modification timestamps or source hashes). If unchanged, it loads the cached bytecode directly, bypassing the expensive lexing + parsing + compilation pipeline. This is especially beneficial for large libraries like numpy or Django where import time would otherwise be significant.

quiz.question: Why does a JIT-compiled language sometimes achieve higher throughput than an equivalent AOT-compiled program for long-running server workloads?
options: JIT compilers always apply more optimisation passes than AOT compilers.
AOT compilers cannot optimise loops, only individual instructions.
A JIT has access to runtime type and branch profile information unavailable to a static AOT compiler, enabling tighter specialisation for the actual workload.
JIT-compiled code runs in a privileged CPU mode unavailable to AOT binaries.
quiz.explanation: A static AOT compiler must generate code that correctly handles all possible inputs and types — it produces correct-for-all-cases code. A JIT compiler observes the actual types and paths used during real execution and generates code optimised for those specific cases. For a loop that always processes 32-bit integers with a predictable branch pattern, JIT-generated code can beat conservative AOT-generated code because the JIT makes speculative bets validated by profiling.

quiz.question: What is the primary portability advantage of a bytecode VM over AOT compilation?
options: Bytecode executes faster than native machine code on modern CPUs.
The same bytecode file runs on any platform that ships the VM, because the VM itself is the architecture-specific component rather than the bytecode.
Bytecode is automatically converted to the optimal machine code for each CPU at download time.
Bytecode files are smaller than AOT binaries because they use compression.
quiz.explanation: Bytecode is defined for an abstract (virtual) machine, not a real CPU. Any real CPU that has a VM implementation can execute the same bytecode without recompilation. Java's 'write once, run anywhere' promise works because `.class` files contain JVM bytecode — the JVM itself (a native binary) handles the architecture-specific execution. AOT binaries are compiled for a specific CPU ISA and cannot run natively on a different architecture.

quiz.question: Which execution strategy is most appropriate for a short-lived command-line tool where instant startup is critical and peak throughput is secondary?
options: JIT compilation, because it achieves the highest throughput
Bytecode VM, because it offers the best portability
Tree-walking interpretation, because it requires no compilation step at all
AOT compilation, because native binaries start without any parse/compile/warmup overhead
quiz.explanation: AOT-compiled binaries (Go, Rust, C) start in microseconds because all compilation happened at build time. For CLI tools, the program may complete its entire task before a JIT even reaches its warmup threshold. JIT's advantage only materialises after warmup, which is irrelevant for short-lived processes. This is explicitly one of Go's design goals: fast startup for CLI and server binaries.

quiz.question: In a stack-based bytecode VM, what is the purpose of the STORE instruction (as implemented in the code examples)?
options: It pops the top value from the stack and saves it into the environment under a given variable name.
It pushes a constant value onto the evaluation stack.
It copies the top of the stack without removing it.
It writes the entire stack contents to disk for the .pyc cache.
quiz.explanation: STORE pops the top value from the evaluation stack and writes it to the environment (variable store) under the specified name. This is how variable assignment works in a stack VM: the right-hand side expression places its result on the stack via PUSH/LOAD/arithmetic instructions, and then STORE transfers that value from the stack into persistent variable storage. The reverse, LOAD, pushes a named variable's value back onto the stack.

quiz.question: What is an 'inline cache' in the context of a JIT-compiled JavaScript engine like V8?
options: A CPU-level cache that stores recently accessed JavaScript strings.
A disk cache that stores JIT-compiled native code between browser restarts.
A mechanism that replaces a generic property-access operation with a specialised fast path based on the observed object shape (hidden class), enabling property reads as direct memory offsets.
A JavaScript developer tool for preloading frequently accessed modules.
quiz.explanation: An inline cache (IC) optimises property access in dynamic languages. When V8 first accesses `obj.x`, it performs a slow hash-table lookup. If it observes that subsequent accesses involve objects with the same hidden class (shape), it patches the access site to use a direct memory-offset read — essentially `load memory[obj_ptr + known_offset]`. This turns a dynamic lookup into a near-zero-cost memory read for the common case where objects have consistent shapes.
